# Welcome

This tutorial walks through an **exome sequencing (WES)** analysis in two modules:

| Module | Question |
|--------|----------|
| **1 — From reads to variants** (this one) | How do raw sequencing reads become a list of variants, and how good is that list? |
| **2 — Somatic mutations in Wilms tumor** | Which genes are mutated in a real pediatric tumor cohort, and do they differ between histologies? |

Module 1 runs the **real command-line tools** of a germline variant-calling pipeline. The grey chunks marked `bash` are shell commands: in RStudio they run exactly like R chunks (the green ▶ arrow), inside the Binder Linux machine, whatever computer you are using.

<div class="alert-info">
**Why only a small region?** A real exome is ~50 million bases sequenced to ~100×: aligning it needs tens of GB of memory and hours of compute. We keep every step identical but restrict the data to **3 million bases of chromosome 11** (11p15.5, the imprinted region containing `IGF2` and `H19`, the locus most frequently altered in Wilms tumor). The full pipeline then runs in under a minute.
</div>

# Part 1 — The Input Files

All inputs are in `data/germline/`, built by `data-prep/build_germline_data.sh`:

| File | What it is |
|------|------------|
| `NA12878_exome_R1.fastq.gz`, `_R2.fastq.gz` | Paired-end reads (2 × 151 bp, Illumina TruSeq exome) of **NA12878**, the most studied human genome, from the **Genome in a Bottle (GIAB)** consortium |
| `reference_chr11p15.fa` | The reference genome sequence (GRCh37) for chromosome 11, positions 1–3,000,000 |
| `exome_targets.bed` | The regions the exome kit was designed to capture |
| `genes_Ensembl87.gff3` | Gene and transcript annotation (Ensembl) |
| `giab_truth.vcf.gz`, `giab_confident.bed` | GIAB's **truth set**: the variants NA12878 really carries, and the regions where that truth is reliable |

<div class="alert-info">
**Why NA12878?** For a patient we never know the "right answer". For NA12878, GIAB has combined many sequencing technologies into a high-confidence set of true variants. Analyzing its exome lets us **measure** how many real variants our pipeline finds and how many false ones it reports, which is impossible with any other sample.
</div>

All outputs go to a `work/` folder:

```{bash make-workdir, echo=TRUE}
mkdir -p work
for tool in fastp bwa samtools bcftools bedtools; do
  printf "%-9s " "$tool"; command -v "$tool"
done
```

## FASTQ: Raw Reads

A FASTQ file stores each read in **4 lines**: an identifier starting with `@`, the bases, a `+` separator, and one **quality** character per base.

```{bash fastq-head, echo=TRUE}
zcat data/germline/NA12878_exome_R1.fastq.gz | head -8
```

```{bash fastq-count, echo=TRUE}
echo "Reads in R1: $(( $(zcat data/germline/NA12878_exome_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))"
echo "Reads in R2: $(( $(zcat data/germline/NA12878_exome_R2.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))"
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Base quality (Phred score).** Each quality character encodes the probability $p$ that the base call is wrong: $Q = -10 \log_{10} p$. Q20 means 1 error in 100, Q30 means 1 in 1,000. The character is the ASCII code of $Q + 33$, so `5` is Q20 and `?` is Q30. (These reads come from a BAM file whose base qualities were already *recalibrated* by GATK, so their quality values look smoother than those of a fresh sequencing run.) In a paired-end run, the read with the same identifier in R1 and R2 comes from the two ends of the same DNA fragment.
</div>

## The Exome Targets

```{bash bed-head, echo=TRUE}
head -5 data/germline/exome_targets.bed
echo "Targets: $(wc -l < data/germline/exome_targets.bed)"
awk '{bp += $3 - $2} END {print "Targeted bases: " bp}' data/germline/exome_targets.bed
```

A **BED** file lists intervals as `chromosome  start  end`, with **0-based** start (the first base of a chromosome is 0) and 1-based end. Only about 9% of our 3 Mb region is targeted: an exome captures the coding exons, ~1–2% of the genome.

# Part 2 — Read QC and Trimming with fastp

`fastp` checks read quality and removes what would hurt the alignment: adapter sequence (when the DNA fragment is shorter than the read), low-quality tails, reads with too many unknown bases (`N`).

```{bash fastp, echo=TRUE}
fastp \
  -i data/germline/NA12878_exome_R1.fastq.gz -I data/germline/NA12878_exome_R2.fastq.gz \
  -o work/trimmed_R1.fastq.gz -O work/trimmed_R2.fastq.gz \
  --detect_adapter_for_pe \
  --json work/fastp.json --html work/fastp.html \
  2> work/fastp.log
tail -n 12 work/fastp.log
```

```{r fastp-summary}
fastp <- fromJSON("work/fastp.json")

kable(
  tibble(
    metric = c("Reads before", "Reads after", "Q30 bases before (%)", "Q30 bases after (%)",
               "Mean read length after (R1)", "Duplication rate (%)", "Reads with adapter trimmed"),
    value  = c(fastp$summary$before_filtering$total_reads, fastp$summary$after_filtering$total_reads,
               round(100 * fastp$summary$before_filtering$q30_rate, 1), round(100 * fastp$summary$after_filtering$q30_rate, 1),
               fastp$summary$after_filtering$read1_mean_length, round(100 * fastp$duplication$rate, 1),
               fastp$adapter_cutting$adapter_trimmed_reads)
  ),
  caption = "fastp summary (the full interactive report is work/fastp.html)."
)
```

```{r plot-quality, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5}
quality_curve <- function(curves, label) {
  tibble(position = seq_along(curves$mean), mean_quality = curves$mean, step = label)
}

bind_rows(
  quality_curve(fastp$read1_before_filtering$quality_curves, "R1 before"),
  quality_curve(fastp$read1_after_filtering$quality_curves,  "R1 after"),
  quality_curve(fastp$read2_before_filtering$quality_curves, "R2 before"),
  quality_curve(fastp$read2_after_filtering$quality_curves,  "R2 after")
) %>%
  separate(step, into = c("read", "stage"), sep = " ") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = position, y = mean_quality, color = stage)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 30, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ read) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(before = "#e74c3c", after = "#2980b9")) +
  labs(x = "Position in read (bp)", y = "Mean base quality (Phred)", color = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**How to read it.** Illumina quality is highest at the start of the read and drops toward the end; **R2 is usually a bit worse than R1**. Most bases above the dashed Q30 line is a good run. Very few reads are removed here: this is a high-quality dataset. Open `work/fastp.html` in the Files pane for the full report.
</div>

# Part 3 — Alignment with BWA-MEM

Alignment finds, for every read, the position in the reference genome it most likely came from. **BWA-MEM** is the standard aligner for short DNA reads. It first needs an **index** of the reference (built once per reference genome):

```{bash bwa-index, echo=TRUE}
cp data/germline/reference_chr11p15.fa work/reference.fa
bwa index work/reference.fa 2> work/bwa_index.log
samtools faidx work/reference.fa
ls work/reference.fa*
```

Then we align, adding a **read group** (`-R`): a tag saying which sample and sequencing run every read belongs to, required by most downstream tools. The output (SAM) is piped directly into `samtools`, which sorts the alignments by position and writes the compressed **BAM** format.

```{bash bwa-mem, echo=TRUE}
bwa mem -t 2 \
  -R '@RG\tID:NA12878_run1\tSM:NA12878\tPL:ILLUMINA\tLB:TruSeq_exome' \
  work/reference.fa work/trimmed_R1.fastq.gz work/trimmed_R2.fastq.gz 2> work/bwa_mem.log |
  samtools fixmate -m - - |
  samtools sort -o work/aligned.bam -
samtools index work/aligned.bam
ls -lh work/aligned.bam
```

<div class="alert-info">
**What `fixmate -m` does.** It adds to every read information about its mate (position, score). The duplicate-marking step below needs it to recognize pairs.
</div>

## Reading a SAM Record

```{bash sam-view, echo=TRUE}
samtools view work/aligned.bam | head -3 | cut -f 1-9
```

The first 9 columns of every alignment:

| # | field | meaning |
|---|-------|---------|
| 1 | QNAME | read name |
| 2 | FLAG | bitwise flags: paired, mapped, reverse strand, first/second in pair... ([decode any value](https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/explain-flags.html)) |
| 3–4 | RNAME, POS | chromosome and leftmost position (1-based) |
| 5 | MAPQ | mapping quality: confidence that the position is right. 60 = unique; 0 = the read fits equally well elsewhere |
| 6 | CIGAR | how the read aligns: `151M` = 151 aligned bases; `I`/`D` = insertion/deletion; `S` = soft-clipped |
| 7–9 | RNEXT, PNEXT, TLEN | mate's chromosome (`=` same), mate's position, fragment length |

## Marking PCR Duplicates

Library preparation amplifies DNA fragments by PCR, so the same original molecule can be sequenced several times. These copies are **not independent evidence**: a PCR error in one copy would look like a variant supported by many reads. `samtools markdup` flags read pairs that start and end at exactly the same positions; variant callers then ignore them.

```{bash markdup, echo=TRUE}
samtools markdup -s work/aligned.bam work/aligned.markdup.bam 2> work/markdup.log
samtools index work/aligned.markdup.bam
grep -E "READ:|DUPLICATE TOTAL" work/markdup.log
```

# Part 4 — Alignment QC

```{bash flagstat, echo=TRUE}
samtools flagstat work/aligned.markdup.bam > work/flagstat.txt
head -n 8 work/flagstat.txt
```

```{bash on-target, echo=TRUE}
total=$(samtools view -c -F 0x904 work/aligned.markdup.bam)
on_target=$(samtools view -c -F 0x904 -L data/germline/exome_targets.bed work/aligned.markdup.bam)
echo -e "mapped_reads\t$total\non_target_reads\t$on_target" | tee work/on_target.tsv
```

```{r on-target-rate}
on_target <- read_tsv("work/on_target.tsv", col_names = c("metric", "reads"), show_col_types = FALSE)
on_target_pct <- round(100 * on_target$reads[2] / on_target$reads[1], 1)
```

**`r on_target_pct`%** of the mapped reads overlap a target. This **on-target rate** measures how well the capture worked: typical exomes reach 60–80%. The rest are "off-target" reads, mostly from DNA flanking the targets.

## Coverage

**Coverage** (or depth) at a position is the number of reads covering it. It is the single most important number for variant calling: a heterozygous variant is seen in about half the reads, so with 4 reads it can easily be missed by chance.

```{bash coverage, echo=TRUE}
# -a: report every targeted position, also those with zero reads.
samtools depth -a -b data/germline/exome_targets.bed work/aligned.markdup.bam > work/target_depth.tsv
head -3 work/target_depth.tsv
```

```{r coverage-summary}
depth <- read_tsv("work/target_depth.tsv", col_names = c("chrom", "pos", "depth"), show_col_types = FALSE)

coverage_summary <- tibble(
  metric = c("Targeted bases", "Mean depth", "Median depth",
             "Bases at >= 1x (%)", "Bases at >= 10x (%)", "Bases at >= 20x (%)"),
  value  = c(nrow(depth), round(mean(depth$depth), 1), median(depth$depth),
             round(100 * mean(depth$depth >= 1), 1), round(100 * mean(depth$depth >= 10), 1),
             round(100 * mean(depth$depth >= 20), 1))
)
kable(coverage_summary, caption = "Coverage over the exome targets (duplicates excluded).")
```

```{r plot-coverage, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5}
depth %>%
  mutate(depth = pmin(depth, 150)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = depth)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "#2980b9", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e74c3c") +
  labs(x = "Depth (capped at 150)", y = "Targeted bases",
       title = "Coverage distribution over the targets; dashed line: 10x") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```

```{r plot-coverage-region, fig.width=11, fig.height=4}
depth %>%
  mutate(bin = floor(pos / 50000) * 50000) %>%
  group_by(bin) %>%
  summarise(mean_depth = mean(depth), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bin / 1e6, y = mean_depth)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#8e44ad") +
  labs(x = "Position on chromosome 11 (Mb)", y = "Mean target depth",
       title = "Mean target depth along the region (50 kb bins)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Coverage is very uneven, and that matters.** Large parts of the targets have few or no reads. 11p15.5 is one of the most **GC-rich** regions of the genome, and GC-rich DNA is captured and amplified poorly. This is a real, well-known limitation of exome sequencing: **a variant in a region with no reads cannot be called, by any software.** We will see its direct consequence in Part 7.
</div>

# Part 5 — Variant Calling with bcftools

At every targeted position, `bcftools mpileup` collects the bases of all reads (the "pileup") and computes **genotype likelihoods**: how probable the observed bases are if the sample is homozygous reference (0/0), heterozygous (0/1), or homozygous alternative (1/1). `bcftools call` then picks the most likely genotype and reports the positions that differ from the reference.

```{bash call, echo=TRUE}
bcftools mpileup -f work/reference.fa -T data/germline/exome_targets.bed \
    -a FORMAT/AD,FORMAT/DP -q 20 -Q 20 work/aligned.markdup.bam 2> /dev/null |
  bcftools call -m -v -Oz -o work/calls.raw.vcf.gz 2> /dev/null
bcftools index -t work/calls.raw.vcf.gz
echo "Raw variant calls: $(bcftools view -H work/calls.raw.vcf.gz | wc -l)"
```

| option | meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `-T targets.bed` | look only at targeted positions |
| `-q 20`, `-Q 20` | ignore reads with mapping quality < 20 and bases with quality < 20 |
| `-a FORMAT/AD,FORMAT/DP` | report allele depths and total depth per sample |
| `call -m` | the multiallelic caller (current default model) |
| `call -v` | output variant sites only |

## Reading a VCF

A **VCF** (Variant Call Format) file has a header (lines starting with `#`) describing every field, then one line per variant.

```{bash vcf-view, echo=TRUE}
bcftools view -H work/calls.raw.vcf.gz | head -3 | cut -f 1-8 | cut -c 1-150
```

```{bash vcf-query, echo=TRUE}
bcftools query -f '%CHROM\t%POS\t%REF\t%ALT\t%QUAL\t[%GT\t%DP\t%AD]\n' work/calls.raw.vcf.gz | head -5
```

The essential columns: `POS` (1-based position), `REF` and `ALT` alleles, `QUAL` (Phred-scaled confidence that the site is variant), and per sample `GT` (genotype: `0/1` heterozygous, `1/1` homozygous alternative), `DP` (depth) and `AD` (reads supporting REF, ALT).

# Part 6 — Filtering, Normalizing and Annotating

## Hard Filters

Raw calls include low-confidence ones. A simple, widely used strategy is to **flag** (not delete) calls with low quality or low depth. They stay in the file with `FILTER = LowQual`, so the decision is documented and reversible.

```{bash filter, echo=TRUE}
bcftools filter -s LowQual -e 'QUAL < 20 || INFO/DP < 10' work/calls.raw.vcf.gz -Oz -o work/calls.filtered.vcf.gz
bcftools index -t work/calls.filtered.vcf.gz
bcftools query -f '%FILTER\n' work/calls.filtered.vcf.gz | sort | uniq -c
```

## Normalizing

The same indel can be written in several ways (e.g. a deletion inside a repeat can be placed at any copy of the repeat). `bcftools norm` puts every variant in a **canonical** form (left-aligned, minimal alleles) and splits multi-allelic sites into one line per allele. Without this, comparing two VCFs (as we do in Part 7) misses identical variants written differently.

```{bash norm, echo=TRUE}
bcftools norm -f work/reference.fa -m -any work/calls.filtered.vcf.gz -Oz -o work/calls.norm.vcf.gz 2> /dev/null
bcftools index -t work/calls.norm.vcf.gz
```

## Variant Statistics

```{bash stats, echo=TRUE}
bcftools stats -f PASS work/calls.norm.vcf.gz > work/calls.stats.txt
grep -E "^SN" work/calls.stats.txt | cut -f 3-
grep -E "^TSTV" work/calls.stats.txt | cut -f 3-5
```

```{r tstv}
tstv <- read_lines("work/calls.stats.txt") %>% str_subset("^TSTV") %>% str_split("\t") %>% pluck(1) %>% `[`(5)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**The Ts/Tv ratio, a free quality check.** Transitions (A↔G, C↔T) are chemically much more frequent than transversions. In **coding** regions the true ratio is about **2.8–3.3** (genome-wide ~2.0–2.1). A value close to 0.5, what random errors would give, signals many false positives.

Here the ratio is **`r tstv`**: between the two. Part of the reason is that the targets also contain UTRs and intronic flanks, where the ratio is lower than in coding exons; part is a cluster of false positives that Part 7 will reveal. With a few hundred variants the ratio is also statistically noisy: it is most useful on a full exome, with tens of thousands.
</div>

## Functional Annotation

Which variants change a protein? `bcftools csq` compares each variant with the gene annotation and predicts its **consequence** on every transcript: synonymous, missense, stop gained, frameshift, splice site, UTR...

```{bash csq, echo=TRUE}
bcftools csq -f work/reference.fa -g data/germline/genes_Ensembl87.gff3 -p a \
  work/calls.norm.vcf.gz -Oz -o work/calls.annotated.vcf.gz 2> /dev/null
bcftools index -t work/calls.annotated.vcf.gz

# One row per variant: position, alleles, genotype, and the consequence on each transcript.
bcftools query -i 'FILTER="PASS"' -f '%POS\t%REF\t%ALT\t%QUAL\t[%GT\t%DP]\t%BCSQ\n' \
  work/calls.annotated.vcf.gz > work/annotated_variants.tsv
```

```{r csq-table}
annotated <- read_tsv("work/annotated_variants.tsv",
                      col_names = c("pos", "ref", "alt", "qual", "genotype", "depth", "bcsq"),
                      col_types = cols(.default = col_character())) %>%
  mutate(across(c(pos, qual, depth), as.numeric))

# BCSQ holds one comma-separated entry per transcript: consequence|gene|transcript|biotype|strand|aa_change|dna_change.
# A leading "*" marks a consequence shared with another variant of the same haplotype.
consequences <- annotated %>%
  separate_longer_delim(bcsq, ",") %>%
  separate_wider_delim(bcsq, "|", names = c("consequence", "gene", "transcript", "biotype", "strand", "aa_change", "dna_change"),
                       too_few = "align_start", too_many = "drop") %>%
  mutate(consequence = str_remove(consequence, "^\\*")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(gene), consequence != ".")

# Most severe consequence per variant, in a simplified order of severity.
severity <- c("stop_gained", "frameshift", "splice_acceptor", "splice_donor", "start_lost", "stop_lost",
              "inframe_deletion", "inframe_insertion", "missense", "splice_region", "synonymous",
              "5_prime_utr", "3_prime_utr", "non_coding", "intron")

worst <- consequences %>%
  mutate(rank = match(word(consequence, 1, sep = "&"), severity)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(rank)) %>%
  group_by(pos, ref, alt) %>%
  slice_min(rank, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()
```

```{r plot-consequences, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
worst %>%
  count(consequence) %>%
  mutate(consequence = fct_reorder(consequence, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = consequence)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#16a085") +
  labs(x = "Variants (PASS)", y = NULL, title = "Most severe predicted consequence per variant") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```

```{r table-protein-changing}
datatable(
  worst %>%
    filter(consequence %in% severity[1:9]) %>%
    transmute(position = pos, ref, alt, genotype, depth, gene, consequence, aa_change, transcript),
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel"), pageLength = 10),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "Protein-changing variants (PASS calls, most severe consequence per variant)."
)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**A healthy genome is full of missense variants.** NA12878 is a healthy individual, yet this one genome carries dozens of protein-changing variants in this small region alone: every person carries thousands across the exome. Most are common, harmless polymorphisms. In a real diagnostic analysis, the next step is to filter by **population frequency** (e.g. gnomAD: a variant carried by 20% of healthy people is not the cause of a rare disease) and by predicted pathogenicity, which requires databases far larger than this tutorial.
</div>

# Part 7 — How Good Are Our Calls? Benchmarking Against GIAB

We now compare our PASS calls with the GIAB truth, restricted to the positions where the comparison is fair: **targeted** by the exome kit **and** inside GIAB's **high-confidence** regions.

```{bash eval-regions, echo=TRUE}
bedtools intersect -a data/germline/exome_targets.bed -b data/germline/giab_confident.bed |
  bedtools sort | bedtools merge > work/eval_regions.bed

# Truth and calls in the evaluation regions, normalized the same way.
bcftools view -T work/eval_regions.bed data/germline/giab_truth.vcf.gz |
  bcftools norm -f work/reference.fa -m -any -Oz -o work/truth.eval.vcf.gz 2> /dev/null
bcftools view -f PASS -T work/eval_regions.bed work/calls.norm.vcf.gz -Oz -o work/calls.eval.vcf.gz
bcftools index -t work/truth.eval.vcf.gz
bcftools index -t work/calls.eval.vcf.gz

awk '{bp += $3 - $2} END {print "Evaluated bases: " bp}' work/eval_regions.bed
```

`bcftools isec` splits the two files into three groups: variants **only in the truth** (false negatives, FN: real variants we missed), **only in our calls** (false positives, FP: calls that are not real), and **in both** (true positives, TP). `-c none` requires position, REF and ALT to match exactly.

```{bash isec, echo=TRUE}
rm -rf work/isec_all
bcftools isec -c none -p work/isec_all work/truth.eval.vcf.gz work/calls.eval.vcf.gz
for f in 0000 0001 0002; do echo "$f: $(grep -vc '^#' work/isec_all/$f.vcf)"; done
```

```{r benchmark-function}
benchmark <- function(dir) {
  n <- map_int(c("0000", "0001", "0002"), ~ sum(!str_starts(read_lines(file.path(dir, paste0(.x, ".vcf"))), "#")))
  tibble(TP = n[3], FN = n[1], FP = n[2]) %>%
    mutate(recall = round(TP / (TP + FN), 3), precision = round(TP / (TP + FP), 3),
           F1 = round(2 * recall * precision / (recall + precision), 3))
}
bench_all <- benchmark("work/isec_all")
kable(bench_all, caption = "All evaluation regions. Recall = TP / (TP + FN): the fraction of real variants found. Precision = TP / (TP + FP): the fraction of our calls that are real.")
```

Recall is low. Why did we miss so many real variants? Look at the depth of our alignment at the missed positions:

```{bash fn-depth, echo=TRUE}
grep -v '^#' work/isec_all/0000.vcf | awk 'BEGIN{OFS="\t"} {print $1, $2 - 1, $2}' > work/missed.bed
samtools depth -a -b work/missed.bed work/aligned.markdup.bam > work/missed_depth.tsv
```

```{r plot-fn-depth, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
missed_depth <- read_tsv("work/missed_depth.tsv", col_names = c("chrom", "pos", "depth"), show_col_types = FALSE)

missed_depth %>%
  mutate(depth_class = cut(depth, c(-1, 0, 4, 9, Inf), labels = c("0", "1–4", "5–9", ">= 10"))) %>%
  count(depth_class) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = depth_class, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#e74c3c") +
  labs(x = "Read depth at the missed variant", y = "Missed variants (FN)",
       title = paste0("Depth at the ", nrow(missed_depth), " missed true variants")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Most missed variants have zero reads.** They were never sequenced, so no caller could find them: the limit is the **data**, not the software. This is why every serious exome report states its **callable regions** (e.g. positions with ≥ 10× coverage) and why a "negative" exome never fully excludes a variant in a poorly covered gene.
</div>

Repeating the benchmark only where we had **at least 10 reads** measures the pipeline itself:

```{bash callable, echo=TRUE}
samtools depth -a -b work/eval_regions.bed work/aligned.markdup.bam |
  awk 'BEGIN{OFS="\t"} $3 >= 10 {print $1, $2 - 1, $2}' |
  bedtools merge > work/callable.bed
awk '{bp += $3 - $2} END {print "Callable bases (>= 10x): " bp}' work/callable.bed

bcftools view -T work/callable.bed work/truth.eval.vcf.gz -Oz -o work/truth.callable.vcf.gz
bcftools view -T work/callable.bed work/calls.eval.vcf.gz -Oz -o work/calls.callable.vcf.gz
bcftools index -t work/truth.callable.vcf.gz
bcftools index -t work/calls.callable.vcf.gz
rm -rf work/isec_callable
bcftools isec -c none -p work/isec_callable work/truth.callable.vcf.gz work/calls.callable.vcf.gz
```

```{r benchmark-callable}
bench_callable <- benchmark("work/isec_callable")
kable(bind_rows(`All evaluation regions` = bench_all, `Callable (>= 10x)` = bench_callable, .id = "regions"),
      caption = "Benchmark against the GIAB truth set.")
```

Where the data are adequate, the pipeline finds nearly every real variant. What about the false positives?

```{bash fp-list, echo=TRUE}
bcftools query -f '%POS\t%REF\t%ALT\t%QUAL\t[%DP]\n' work/isec_callable/0001.vcf > work/false_positives.tsv
```

```{r fp-genes}
genes <- read_tsv("data/germline/genes_Ensembl87.gff3", comment = "#", col_names = FALSE, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  filter(X3 == "gene") %>%
  transmute(start = X4, end = X5, gene = str_match(X9, "Name=([^;]+)")[, 2])

false_positives <- read_tsv("work/false_positives.tsv", col_names = c("pos", "ref", "alt", "qual", "depth"),
                            show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(gene = paste(genes$gene[genes$start <= pos & genes$end >= pos], collapse = ", "),
         gene = if_else(gene == "", "(outside annotated genes)", gene)) %>%
  ungroup()

kable(count(false_positives, gene, name = "false_positives", sort = TRUE),
      caption = "Genes containing the false-positive calls (callable regions).")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**False positives cluster in difficult genes.** Most of them fall in `MUC5B` (and other mucin genes), made of long, nearly identical **tandem repeats**: short reads cannot be placed unambiguously, and small misalignments look like variants. They pass our filters with good quality and depth. Every pipeline struggles with such regions; real projects either exclude them (GIAB publishes "difficult region" lists) or confirm variants there with another technology (e.g. Sanger or long reads) before reporting them.
</div>

# Summary

| step | tool | output |
|------|------|--------|
| Read QC and trimming | `fastp` | trimmed FASTQ + QC report |
| Alignment | `bwa mem` | BAM |
| Duplicate marking | `samtools fixmate` / `markdup` | BAM with duplicates flagged |
| Alignment QC | `samtools flagstat` / `depth` | on-target rate, coverage |
| Variant calling | `bcftools mpileup` / `call` | raw VCF |
| Filtering and normalization | `bcftools filter` / `norm` | clean VCF |
| Annotation | `bcftools csq` | consequences on genes |
| Benchmarking | `bedtools`, `bcftools isec` | recall, precision |

The main lessons: **coverage limits recall** far more than the caller does, and **false positives concentrate in repetitive genes**. Module 2 moves from one germline genome to a cohort of tumors.
